speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement regarding the purchase of uranium ore.
On March 16, 1948, I announced to the house the policies which had been established in connection with the purchase of uranium in ores and concentrates. These policies involved the establishment of a minimum price which was guaranteed for five years from March 31, 1948. With a view to encouraging further prospecting for radioactive minerals, I announced on December 20, 1948, that the period of the guarantee had been extended by two years, that is, until March 31, 1955. In recent weeks the advisory mining committee on radioactive minerals has been giving consideration to a possible further extension of the guarantee period. The committee has recommended that the period of the guarantee be extended to Mardh 31, 1958, and the government has concurred in that recommendation. It is hoped that this further extension will provide an additional incentive to the search for radioactive ores.
In my announcement of March 16, 1948, I stated that the price for the uranium content of ores or concentrates would be at the minimum rate of $2.75 per pound of contained UsOs f.o.to. rail. I stated further-and I quote from my announcement:
Under special circumstances consideration may be given to the payment of a higher price or to the acceptance of ores or concentrates of a lower grade.
In response to numerous inquiries regarding the application of this special price provision of the purchasing policy, Eldorado Mining and Refining (1944) Limited, the designated purchasing agent for uranium in ores or concentrates, has now established a formula to be used as the basis for negotiating special prices. The details of the formula will be announced shortly by Eldorado Mining and Refining (1944) Limited.
The extension of the period during which a guaranteed price will apply, combined with definite information as to the basis of establishing special prices, will, I think, be helpful to the mining interests concerned with the production of uranium ore.

subtopic: PURCHASE BY C. P. R. OF SHAWINIGAN FALLS TERMINAL RAILWAY CAPITAL STOCK
PURCHASE BY C. P. R. OF SHAWINIGAN FALLS TERMINAL RAILWAY CAPITAL STOCK
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 88, respecting the purchase by Canadian Pacific Railway Company of shares of the capital stock of the Shawinigan Falls Terminal Railway Company.

subtopic: PURCHASE BY C. P. R. OF SHAWINIGAN FALLS TERMINAL RAILWAY CAPITAL STOCK
speechtext: Will the hon. member explain the bill?

subtopic: PURCHASE BY C. P. R. OF SHAWINIGAN FALLS TERMINAL RAILWAY CAPITAL STOCK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not believe the purpose of this bill is such as to justify any lengthy explanation on my part. It deals with a very simple matter which I believe is of limited importance, and which would attract very little attention on the part of the general public. The purpose of the bill is to permit the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to purchase the capital stock of the Shawinigan Falls Terminal Railway Company. By virtue of the Railway Act, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is not authorized to purchase the capital stock of another railway company, and the purpose of this bill is to provide legislative authority for this to be done.
The Shawinigan Falls Terminal Railway Company is a small company operating entirely within the province of Quebec. It was incorporated in 1902 by provincial statute, at which time the capital stock of $200,000 was divided into shares of $100 each. In 1906 the authorized capital was increased to $300,000, the additional $100,000 again being issued in shares of $100 each. This company owns approximately a third of a mile of line, and perhaps a little more than a mile of sidings which are used by industrial concerns in that area, and to carry on its operations it owns and maintains four electric locomotives. Its operations are very simple, consisting of placing on the sidings of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific the cars used by industries in that neighbourhood.
Shawinigan Falls Railway
Until recent years it was found advisable to have this operation conducted on that basis; in other words it was considered economical and advantageous to industry, as well as to the advantage of both major railway companies, to have this work done by the terminal railway. In late years, however, the situation has altered materially, for many reasons, so that it is now practically impossible for this small company to operate effectively. The four electric locomotives are in poor condition and would have to be replaced, and the power to operate them is no longer available. The Shawinigan Water and Power Company, which in fact owns all the shares of the terminal railway company, had surplus power which it could sell to the railway company, and this permitted the railway company to operate. Today, however, the power company has no surplus of power, as a result of the great industrial development that has taken place in that area. For these reasons, and others of less importance, following study and negotiations by both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, it has been decided that the operation could be more effectively carried out by the large railway companies themselves. Instead of using electric locomotives, as the terminal railway company did, they will use diesel engines, which will produce better results and give more efficient service.
That, I think, generally explains the purpose of the bill. I should add that the purchase is to be made by both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, each company paying half the purchase price. As I said before, the capital stock has a face value of $300,000, but the purchase price is to be $125,000, to be paid in equal proportions by the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific. In other words each company will pay approximately $62,500 for the capital stock of this terminal railway company. As I stated earlier, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company requires authorization from parliament to make this purchase, while the Canadian National already has authority by virtue of its own act. If hon. members will look at the explanatory note they will see that section 147 of the Railway Act prohibits the Canadian Pacific from making such purchases, while on the other hand if they refer to the legislation setting up the Canadian National Railways they will see that it authorizes purchases of this kind.
If any other information should be required I think it might be better obtained from the representatives of both major railway companies when this bill is referred to the appropriate standing committee.

The house resumed, from Monday, April 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Maybank for the second reading of Bill No. 7, respecting Alberta Natural Gas Company, and the motion of Mr. MacDougall: "That this question be now put".

Mr. Speaker, this bill, and Bill No. 9, have been debated for a considerable length of time, both this session and last session. During the course of the debate many strong arguments have been put forward as to why these bills should not be passed in their present form. No one supporting the bills has effectively answered those arguments. At this stage in the proceedings I do not propose to take the time to repeat the arguments against the bills, but I would say that those of us who have opposed them, and are still opposed to them, have endeavoured to show why the object of the two companies seeking incorporation-that is, the building of a pipe line to carry natural gas from Alberta to the west coast, running for its main length through the United States-is not in the best interests of Canada.
I may say that we have had considerable success in securing support for our views, if not in this house, at least throughout the country. This has been illustrated by the numerous editorials and other articles which have appeared in the press, as well as the various resolutions passed by organizations and sent to members and governments supporting the views we have put forward. This has been particularly true in the case of British Columbia. As a result I think there is now a considerable body of public opinion strongly opposed to the building of a gas pipe line the major portion of which will run through the United States rather than through Canada. This being so, I believe that, no matter what may be done on second reading of these two bills, public opinion will prevent the building of a line through the United States, even though it seems to be the intention of the government and its supporters in this house to push the bills through in their present form without any safeguards as to where such pipe lines may be built.
There has been a considerable amount of complaint about the length of time this debate has occupied. The debate has been continued for two reasons. The first was to bring the facts of the matter to public attention, and that has been done. As I have already stated,


the result has been that a great deal of support has been stirred up for an all-Canadian route. Second, we had hoped that the companies concerned would announce their intention of building the line entirely within Canada. Such an announcement has not been made by either of the companies, so that we have been disappointed in that hope. Although on numerous occasions it has been stated that all that was required to remove our opposition to this bill was an announcement on the part of the incorporators that the line would run through Canada, no such announcement has been made. This indicates strongly that the company intends, if at all possible, to build the line in the United States. In view of that we must continue to oppose that purpose, and I trust that when the vote is taken on both these bills all members of this house who place Canada's interests first will vote against them.
During the past ten days the majority of members have been back in their constituencies, and have thus had an opportunity of finding out what their constituents think about it. It have no doubt that, as a result, some members will have changed their minds in connection with these bills, and will have come to the point where they can see that they must oppose the bills in their present form.
During the course of this debate government supporters have had recourse to the old trick of attempting to draw a red herring across the real issue by raising the cry of monopoly. The speeches in support of these bills during the two weeks immediately before the Easter recess practically all concentrated on that cry of "monopoly, monopoly." It was stated that by opposing these bills we were encouraging or setting up a monopoly. This was an attempt on the part of the supporters of these bills to place those of us who opposed them in the position of encouraging monopolies.
Such an attempt is shown for what it really is, by the fact that we have given repeated pledges that we will withdraw our opposition if the companies will announce their intention to build the line through Canada; therefore we are not trying to encourage monopolies. I do not think anyone in this house has any such idea. The matter is just as simple as that.
As soon as any company, it does not matter which one, undertakes to build a pipe line through Canada, it will receive my support and I believe the support of everyone in this house. Time and again the argument has been put forward that since one company already has a charter which does not specify a Canadian route, every other company which

applies for a charter should receive a similar one. Such an argument means that because a mistake was made when the first company applied for a charter, we should continue that mistake. That is poor logic. Many of us have said that the mistake was made when the general pipe lines bill was put through without a provision that the route must be specified before a charter is granted. We have also said many times that we believe it was a mistake to grant the Westcoast Transmission Company a charter without the route being specified. The fact that those mistakes were made is certainly no excuse for repeating them in this case.
Immediately before Easter one speaker suggested that the Westcoast Transmission Company had tried to deceive parliament by giving a committee of this house an assurance that a route would be built from the northern part of Alberta through British Columbia to Vancouver, and that no reliance could be placed on that statement. Associated with that statement was the matter of another application made by that company to build a line from the southern part of Alberta down through the United States. An attempt was made to show that this company was not acting in good faith, since it had repeatedly announced its intention to build a line through the Yellowhead pass to Vancouver. It is not my purpose to defend any particular company, but I think the issue should be considered in a fair manner. All that needs to be done is to examine the representations which have been made on the application made by this company to the Alberta natural gas and oil conservation board, the sittings of which have occupied some weeks. The reasons given during the hearings, the data and everything else that was given in connection with the building of the gas pipe line from Edmonton, indicated that it would go through the Yellowhead pass to the coast.
As I say, to anyone familiar with these proceedings this is quite sufficient to dispel any idea that this other company is acting in had faith. All these arguments in connection with monopoly and in connection with this other company are entirely aside from the main issue, which is whether the line will be built in Canada and thus serve the maximum number of Canadians, or whether it will be built mainly in the United States and thus will serve a minimum number of Canadians and provide a minimum amount of employment for our own people.

Mr. Speaker, when I last spoke in the debate I felt that one or two points in connection with criticism concerning the stand taken by the group to which I belong should be cleared up. Criticism has been made of small minorities in the house for exercising what, to my mind, is the right of all minorities, that of expressing themselves in the only way possible, namely by speaking and by talking about the subject under discussion. It is true there is a limit to what can be done and that limit is the patience of the government to wait until our speakers are exhausted. That point has just about been reached. I do not think the hon. member meant to suggest for one moment that minorities have no rights in this house. It is true that he did not suggest that might is right, but he might as well have said it because of the manner in which he referred to the action taken by the minority in regard to this bill.
I take strong exception to the way in which this bill has been presented. For two sessions now we have not been able to change it one iota. All we are asking is that a Canadian route be guaranteed, but we are told that we must accept the bill as it is. This is not the only raw material we are shipping from Canada to the United States in order to help build up that country. I have in mind lumber, ore and pulp. These materials are

being sent to the United States where they are being fabricated into high-priced commodities. Naturally our Canadian youth follow the raw materials because they find more attractive pay and working conditions in connection with their fabrication than are to be found in the saw mills and mines of Canada. We should keep our raw materials in Canada to build up our own industries. We should encourage our youth to develop a Canadian concept of society rather than a United States concept. They should be encouraged to stay with us and develop our own country.
Reference has been made already to the homes and communities that would be built up in western Canada and I do not intend to repeat those arguments. In British Columbia-this is possibly true of the other provinces-there is a good deal of unemployment at the present time. We have not done a great deal to solve our unemployment problem through the development of our own industries. I do believe that if this pipe line were constructed through the interior of British Columbia the development that would follow would entirely wipe out unemployment in that province. Not only would it do that; it would help to balance our economy and conserve United States dollars.
On the other hand the claim is made that a monopoly is being built up by allowing this one company to carry on, although, there are two companies now. The very nature of a gas pipe line is a monopoly the way things are handled today. Once the gas crosses the border and is in the hands of the United States distributors a monopoly is created. I should like to quote a statement made by Senator Gillette in the United States Senate as reported in the Congressional Record of Monday, March 20, 1950. He was dealing with the question of monopolies based on pipe lines and he referred to the throttle-hold on society which these monopolistic enterprises had. Reference has been made to the vast empire we are throwing away by allowing this commodity to go into the United States, because once it has reached that country it will be helping to develop industry there. Referring to monopolies, Senator Gillette states:
I think there is no question about that. I thank the Senator from Illinois. It is very evident that these producers, astute businessmen as they are, are not throwing money down a rathole. They know exactly what they are doing.
Referring again to the threats I mentioned a few moments ago-in plain English-what is meant is that they will go out on strike. They will go out on strike not because they cannot make money on their sales of natural gas in interstate commerce. They are making a great deal of money, as the Senator from Illinois has pointed out. They will go on strike because they cannot make all the money the traffic will bear. They will go on strike, let the
Prairie Transmission Lines gas stay in the wells, or go sailing off into the clouds, make not a nickel on the gas sales, but prevent consumers from obtaining a cubic foot of it to heat homes and cook meals, and they will continue making plenty of money on their oil production, letting the gas consumption go by.
What they are telling the American public, in effect, is that if they are not privileged to sell a product on which they have an almost total monopoly at the price they demand-the American public will simply have to bear with it the best it can.
This is a boycott which. I am sure, the American people will not endure. Indeed, any concerted effort by a group of producers to withhold their product from interstate commerce would be an illegal boycott subject to prosecution under the antitrust laws.
Somehow, I cannot believe that the threat is anything more than implied. I cannot seriously believe that any such threat would be carried out.
And again:
Surely those who imply such a threat, who even hint at it, know that what they are asking for, in return, is legislation of a character so drastic as to make them yearn for the good old days when they had nothing to worry about but federal power commission regulation of rates on the sale- just the sale of gas into interstate commerce-not the whole production and gathering of the product.
I wonder if possibly they are requesting the congress to retaliate by removing the bounty placed on oil and gas production through repeal of the annual 27J-cent depletion allowance on petroleum?
He ends up with a comment which covers the whole argument, as follows:
Monopoly as generally understood means control of a product both as to quantity allowed to reach the market and price. If you control the quantity you automatically control the price. Hence, the petroleum industry can be set down as definitely a monopoly.
And again:
There is no need1 to cite chapter and verse on the character of this industry. It is enough to note that it is increasingly dominated by a few giant corporations which own and control one of the most vital natural resources modern man has ever discovered.
I merely quote that to show the value that was placed by the United States congress on a commodity which we are handing over so lightly to anyone who cares to purchase it. Not very long ago a royal commission was appointed to investigate the Alberta oil industry, and I should like to quote a very apt reference that was made in that report:
The importance to a nation of available reserves of oil is emphasized by the following quotations. Mr. Coolidge, a former president of the United States, said:
"It is even probable that the supremacy of nations may be determined by the possession of available petroleum and its products."
A memorandum to the French government after the last great war, of its wartime oil commissioner, Mr. Berenger, is said to have contained the following passage:
"He who owns the oil will own the world, for he will rule the sea by means of the heavy oils, the air by means of the ultra refined oils, and the land

Prairie Transmission Lines by means of petrol and the illuminating oils. And in addition to these he will rule his fellow men in an economic sense, by reason of the fantastic wealth he will derive from oil-the wonderful substance which is more sought after and more precious today than gold itself."
I quote that merely to show the value of the commodity with which we are dealing today. I plead, as has the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), that there be a reconsideration of the decision regarding this bill. Before this bill reaches the committee I should like to see the company change its attitude. I trust that public opinion will force them to do what we are asking them to do. Before concluding I want to say that I know nothing about the personnel of this company. I do not know anything about the financial arrangements of the individuals concerned or anything else. I am fighting solely for my own province. I have faith in my province, and the legislature of that province has unanimously supported the stand we take. The Canadian Legion, boards of trade, individuals and communities throughout the whole of British Columbia have pleaded and begged their members, irrespective of politics, to support the attitude taken by this group in favour of an all-Canadian route. I am afraid if we do not fight for our province they will take the bait that is dangled before them by some of the United States members of congress. I have a copy of the Congressional Record for March 9, 1950, and I should like to quote a portion of a letter read into the record by the Hon. Hugh Butler of Nebraska. In it are these words:
My idea in writing to you is this. We Americans care nothing for the political angles, but what is best for all of us for our betterment as a whole and national safety problems. I have read many times of Canadians wanting to join us, provinces or certain districts. Why not start negotiations to see if British Columbia would vote to join us and make Columbia our forty-ninth state. Then Alaska would become the fiftieth state. This is the best method to keep our borders contiguous and realistic in adding new states. Otherwise, to make far-away places or islands, states, is laughable. This would make it possible to better build up our coast defences of the west in radar and landing fields. Hope this sounds sensible . . . I
I merely read that into the record to show that there is >a feeling on the Pacific coast that we are neglected by the parliament at Ottawa. Our needs are not properly considered, and I feel on the question of these pipe line measures our needs are definitely not being properly considered because not one member of the cabinet has given any intimation that he would support our point of view and assist us in getting the line constructed through British Columbia. In conclusion, I want to plead again with this company to reconsider their application, and

before it is too late to insert in it a promise to go through the province of British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, in the rather long debate that has taken place on these two measures I have only taken a small part of the time. I am not claiming that there is any virtue in .that. Perhaps it is the other way around because I am convinced that the debate that has taken place on these bills has served a useful purpose. I have just returned from the province of British Columbia where I spent the Easter recess, and I know that the people of that province are concerned about the route that the proposed pipe line will take. If other members from British Columbia receive the resolutions and letters from important public bodies and individuals that I receive, they must be aware of how the people of British Columbia feel. I am not under any illusion that anything I will say is going to affect the course of government policy in this matter, because in my opinion, the bill is a private bill only in name. As for the attitude towards them on the government side of the house, they are certainly government measures. The government will see to it that they pass.
There is, unfortunately I think, a feeling in this country that our resources are unlimited. Almost every day public speakers at various functions refer to "Canada's unlimited natural resources". Canada's natural resources are far from being unlimited, and the same is true of the natural resources of the American continent as a whole. In the country to the south of us they are getting rather scarce because the people of the United States have been more assiduous in developing and exploiting them than we have. For that reason alone we should be very careful how our natural resources are going to be developed, and who is going to benefit by their development.
I am convinced that if this natural gas pipe line goes first through United States territory, serving the lower mainland of British Columbia last, the United States will benefit more than Canada from a Canadian natural resource. That is my main reason for drawing the matter to the attention of the house again, in order to see if it will not even now exercise not only its prerogative but its duty to protect the interests of the Canadian people. Among the large number of resolutions I have received there are two that have come to hand within the last three weeks which I wish to put on the record. I do so for two reasons. The institutions which have passed the resolutions are important ones in the life of the province

of British Columbia, and I have been a member of both of them for a long number of years. The first resolution I wish to read to the house is one passed by the city council of the city of Vancouver which I received in a letter under date of March 29, 1950. The letter including the resolution is signed by the city clerk and reads:
I wish to notify you of the following resolution passed by the Vancouver city council on March 27, 1950:
"That the city council advise the federal government of its opinion that the routing of a gas pipe line through British Columbia is imperative for the industrial development of the regional area through Vancouver. Further, that the Vancouver members of parliament be forwarded a copy of this resolution and their support solicited."
There are no C.C.F. members on the Vancouver city council. They are Liberals and Conservatives, supporters of the government and supporters-*
Non-partisans.

Oh, yes, non-partisans. I know how non-partisan they are, and if you want to go into that I will gladly do it. They are non-partisan in the morning when they are addressing the city council; they are Liberal or Progressive Conservative in the afternoon when they are addressing meetings of those parties and they are coalitionists in the evening when they are addressing a coalition meeting. If you want any more I can give it to you. I know what "non-partisan" means, and it is pure bunk. They are members supporting the opposition and the government; but in respect to this resolution they are unanimous. They ask this government to see that the pipe line goes through British Columbia and serves that province first. It seems to me that this long debate has served a useful purpose. I have in my hand a clipping from the Vancouver Province of April 12, which would be last Wednesday, containing a short comment on a letter received by the city council, I assume in response to a copy of this resolution, which reads:
Vancouver gas needs come first
City council was assured Tuesday by Reconstruction Minister Howe that Vancouver natural gas requirements will be met before gas is exported to to the United States.
If that does not mean that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has decided that the pipe line will go through British Columbia first, it is merely double talk.
That is what it is.

Certainly the people of British Columbia have been given the impression that their needs will be met first, and that can only be done if the pipe line goes through 55946-103
Prairie Transmission Lines British Columbia first. If that is not done a letter like this is simply an attempt to deceive the people of that province.
The next resolution I have is from the Vancouver, New Westminster and district trades and labour council, a body of responsible trade unionists interested in British Columbia affairs. They are interested in having this pipe line constructed in British Columbia because they are concerned among other things with the employment situation. As hon. members know, last winter there was a great deal of unemployment in British Columbia, and although the situation is not as bad today many are still out of work. So it is understandable that the delegates to this trades and labour council, I imagine representing more than half the labour force in British Columbia, would be interested in the route to be followed by the proposed pipe line. Their resolution was as follows:
Whereas an all-Canadian route for the proposed natural gas pipe line from Alberta to British Colum-bit will help control the gas in Canada until most Canadians have first been served: and,
Whereas employment will result in Canada both from construction and future maintenance than any other proposed route.
Therefore be it resolved that this Vancouver, New Westminster and district trades and labour council strongly urge the dominion government to authorize the proposed all-Canadian route.
And be it further resolved that copies of this resolution, be sent to Prime Minister St. Laurent, members of the dominion cabinet, and to B.C. members of parliament.
I considered it important, Mr. Speaker, that some British Columbia member should put on record the views of the Vancouver city council and of one of the central labour bodies in this matter, in order that hon. members might learn of them before the final vote on the bill now before us.
Statements have been made from time to time by hon. members supporting these bills that it would be desirable to have the pipe lines go through the United States because if that were done the construction cost would be less. Surely that is a weak argument in a matter of this kind. If we wanted to deal with all our natural resources in that way I imagine cheaper routes and easier disposition of our resources could be found in the United States; but if that were done the greatest advantage from those natural resources would go to the United States. I noticed that the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. MacDougall) took that position when he addressed a meeting in Vancouver during the Easter holidays. The report of that meeting, which is rather brief, states:
Dr. MacDougall said: "If the line goes through the U.S., Vancouver will get the gas cheaper, because the Americans will help pay for the cost of the line."

Prairie Transmission Lines
There we are told that if Vancouver is to get the gas more cheaply, the United States must get the greater part of the gas, and that therefore the pipe line must go first through the United States. I should like to know who is right, or who is giving the most nearly correct information. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said Vancouver would be served first; the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard said Vancouver would be served best if it were served last. This would be really funny if it were not so tragic. It is regrettable that some of our people are so anxious to give away our natural resources.
I think this is the time-it may be too late when we are in committee-for British Columbia members to show some regard for the opinion of the people of British Columbia and see to. it that when this pipe line is built it will serve the residents of Canada first.

Mr. Speaker, thanks to the wonderful development of aviation I was able to leave Vancouver yesterday morning and arrive in Ottawa last evening. After spending a week in my home city I became convinced that I could do no less for the people of Vancouver-Quadra, regardless of their party affiliations, and in fact for the people of British Columbia as a whole, than give a brief summing up of this pipe line argument before these two bills are sent to committee.
Before going on to do that may I express the hope that at least some of the Liberal members from British Columbia will rise during this debate and tell us what they think of this question. Not one Liberal member has spoken on this particular bill, so they all have the opportunity of stating their stand. In view of the extent to which the interests of British Columbia are involved in this matter, I challenge those members to state their position on this pipe line bill.
The bill we are now discussing is described as an act to incorporate Prairie Transmission Lines Limited. I believe that this particular bill is an orphan. At the moment the sponsor of the bill is not in the chamber. It has even lost its father. He is not sufficiently interested to listen to the debate on his bill. It has been interesting to see how this particular bill to incorporate Prairie Transmission Lines Limited has been sidetracked by the government. It always seems to happen that the Alberta Natural Gas Company bill is given priority. Even two weeks ago today when the bill to incorporate Prairie Transmission Lines Limited came up for debate, after the first speech the sponsor of the other bill, who is also a parliamentary assistant,

COMMONS moved that the debate on this Prairie Transmission Lines bill be adjourned. As you know, Mr. Speaker, a vote was called and the sponsor of the Prairie Transmission Lines bill, the member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), did not even vote against the adjournment of his own bill. I repeat, therefore, that this poor bill is an orphan.
This raises an important point. It is obvious that the full weight of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), and the Canadian government as well as the Liberal party, with the exception of the member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), is behind the application of the Alberta Natural Gas Company for incorporation. I suggest that it would be interesting to go a little further into this picture. I think it will be found that a certain financial house in New York, which is behind the applicants for Alberta Natural Gas Company, is the spider in this huge web. That is the spider which is going to devour the people of British Columbia. What is happening here is that United States interests are being aided and abetted by the Canadian government to put this pipe line through the United States on its route to the Pacific coast.
Some of the Liberal members from British Columbia are putting up an alibi by talking monopoly. They would be far wiser to check upon this huge government monopoly, this monopoly composed of the Canadian government and this financial house in New York. There is the real monopoly to be fought. What do we hear? We hear these British Columbia members shouting-
Would the hon. member mind giving us some proof of what he is saying? Is he just bringing charges out of thin air, or has he some proof?
I am saying that behind this proposal there is a New York financial house, and the minister knows which one it is just as well as I do.
I do not.

That evidence was given before the Senate committee last fall, I believe. There is no need for the minister to be coy about the matter, or to suggest nobody knows about it. It is common knowledge. There is the real monopoly that threatens the people of British Columbia. Yet we have these Liberal members setting up a straw man, by saying that those of us who are opposing the proposal that the route of the pipe line should be through the United States are really fighting for a monopoly.
The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) took that stand in British Columbia just ten days

ago. I have here a dispatch from the Vancouver Sun, dated April 6, 1950. The heading is "Two Pipe Lines all Canada can stand." The minister, when he was interviewed on this question, got out of it-
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. This house is now adjourned because there is not a quorum.
No, there is not a quorum.

speechtext:
The
member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) has the floor.

I was discussing the interview given by the Minister of Fisheries when he was in Vancouver a few days ago. He has now reached the conclusion that there should be two pipe lines, one to go through Canada and one to go through the United States. This is the first time that anyone has-

I do not mind the hon. gentleman making a speech, but I do object to his quoting from a paper what I am alleged to have said. In this case it is entirely wrong; I said nothing of the kind. I know of no difference in the pipe line bills presented to this house. So far as I am concerned, they can all go through the house, and the best deal that we can get out of all the applications should be the one we choose.
Prairie Transmission Lines
They have not all been the same, because the one company that secured incorporation gave a pledge it would build the line through Canada.

I should like to ask the hon. gentleman a question. If I were your client, would you tell me that the pledge the company gave would bind the company and its successors in future years as to where the pipe line would be built? Would you say that the company is compelled to build that pipe line in Canada?

It is not a question of future years. The company gave a pledge that this pipe line would be built through Canada. In my opinion that pledge is binding. If the company does not fulfil the pledge, then it will certainly be worthy of the utmost censure, and I will be one of. those who will censure it; of course it is unfortunate that the government, in providing for these pipe line charters, did not insist on having the routes stated in the bills. But the point I am making is this. That company would never have got a charter if they had not given a pledge that they were going to build through Canada.
If the sponsor of this bill will get up and say that he has the assurance from them that they are going to build this pipe line in Canada now, I will certainly support your recommendations here.

If the sponsor of this bill stood up in the house and pledged that this company would build their line through Canada first, I would have no further objection to the bill; although I think it would be much wiser for parliament to insist that this provision should be written into each of the charters and also that the Pipe Lines Act itself should be amended.
If they were serious in their pledge, they would agree to that now.
I did not hear what the minister said.
I said that in my opinion if they were sincere in their pledge that they were going to build the pipe line through Canada they would be the ones who would be asking to have their bill changed.

The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) said two or three weeks ago that the Westcoast Transmission Company would be perfectly ready to have their charter amended to that effect.
I must, however, get back to this question of the shadow monopoly which is being talked about especially by the British Columbia Liberal members. I do not blame them because this is the only excuse they have for their

Prairie Transmission Lines stand on these bills. They have had a hard time to think up arguments. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) is quoted as having said:
Some members are opposed to a monopoly, but they also demand that only one company get a franchise.
Nobody in this house has demanded that only one company get a franchise. That statement by the Minister of Fisheries, if he is correctly reported, is entirely misleading. What everyone who has opposed the pipe line bills has said is that any group of applicants for a charter who will come in and say they will build their line through British Columbia will get their bill through without any difficulty. But the applicants for these two bills, the Alberta Natural Gas Company and the Prairie Transmission Lines Limited, have so far been extremely careful not to give any such undertaking.
Then about a week ago we had the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing) quoted as making a similar statement. Radio reports were to the effect that he had said that those who were opposing these bills were only fighting for a monopoly. If he said that, he knew it was utter tommyrot because such has not been the case. Then we had the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode) quoted as making a certain statement; and incidentally it would be interesting to know to what spot he has disappeared this afternoon. He was in the house earlier in the proceedings, but when the vote on the last bill was called he was not to be found. It will be interesting to see whether he is here for the vote on this particular bill. He is quoted in the press of April 11 as follows:
Mr. Goode said he and all other B.C. Liberal M.P.'s-with the exception of George Cruickshank-
Who of course has been a great problem child for the other British Columbia Liberal members.
-were opposed to any bill which would grant a monopoly to any natural gas company in western Canada for a pipe line.
And there were similar statements by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. MacDougall). He is quoted as saying:
We are faced with a complete positive monopoly of the Pipe Lines Act by a private company unless the charter is granted to the other companies. That one company was granted the charter and the other refused is not democratic.
All these Liberal members know that the reason, and the sole reason, one company obtained a charter was that they pledged themselves to build through Canada. I therefore repeat that this talk of monopoly by

these government supporters from the province of British Columbia is merely a little bit of shadow-boxing, the setting up of a straw man in order to knock him down.
I was glad to hear some reference today to the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). Two or three weeks ago he was asked a prepared question in the house, and in reply he said that he would not agree to gas being sent to the United States through a pipe line before the pipe line reaches Vancouver. That statement, read according to the ordinary use of the English language, simply means that until the pipe line had been laid right into Vancouver he would not allow any gas to be turned on in the United States. But he has been careful all the way through the piece never to make the statement that he would not grant a permit to a company unless that company laid an all-Canadian route. All he needs to do to stop these debates is to get up in the house and give his pledge that, as the responsible minister, he will see that no permit is granted unless the route is to go through Canada.
Then to come down to the plan of the Prairie Transmission Lines Limited, I have here their petition to this house; and it sets out clearly where they intend to build this pipe line. This is their object:
To construct, maintain, own, operate and use a pipe line or pipe lines to transport natural and artificial gas and oil in, the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia commencing at a point in the general Calgary area in the province of Alberta and thence to a point in the vicinity of Blairmore in the said province and thence to a point in the vicinity of Kingsgate in the province of British Columbia and thence to the United States of America leaving Canada at a point at or near Kingsgate in the said province of British Columbia-
Which is in the far eastern part of the province.
-re-entering Canada in the vicinity of Blaine-
Which is on the coast.
-in the state of Washington and proceeding north to the Vancouver area in the province of British Columbia,-
Since last year they have added these words:
-or to the said destinations by such other route or routes as may be authorized by the board of transport commissioners.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose for the dinner recess I had just completed reading the first objective of these

applicants for incorporation of Prairie Transmission Lines Limited. It sets out the route along which they propose to build a pipe line.
I have here, in addition, a copy of the map filed last fall by these same people in the Senate. I only wish there were some way this map could be reprinted in Hansard, because I believe if hon. members could have a good look at it they would be satisfied that we are on the right side of this case.
In effect, this is a map of the state of Washington. The Canadian boundary appears across the map within a couple of inches of the top. The proposed pipeline starts at Macleod in southern Alberta, goes through the Crowsnest pass following the Canadian Pacific railway line, passes Fernie and Cran-brook, then crosses the American boundary, still in the eastern part of British Columbia. It goes almost due south for well over a hundred miles until it reaches the city of Spokane, which is quite a large city in the state of Washington. Then there is a branch line to the north which crosses the Canadian boundary in order to reach the smelting city of Trail. It goes only about twenty miles over into British Columbia.
Why show it to Newfoundland?

You had better get up and tell your own story about this gas bill. The main line continues past Spokane, toward the coast. About half way from Spokane to the coast there is another branch line, this time to- the south. It goes down to the point where it serves the United States atomic energy plant at Hanford with a branch off to Yakima. Then goes farther south branching off to Walla Walla, and then right down across the boundary of the state of Washington into the state of Oregon. The main line continues out to the coast, which it reaches between Everett and Seattle. Then it turns south and goes to Tacoma, south through Washington, and down to Portland in the state of Oregon. All that British Columbia gets at the coast is a stub line to the north which crosses the boundary into Vancouver. In other words we have the pipe line in Canada for a short distance through the mountains in East Kootenay, and then two small stub lines which come over the boundary at Trail and at Vancouver.
This means, of course, that, so far as development is concerned, this company plan to develop the states of Washington and Oregon. As a matter of fact I do not think they are concerned what places they develop. All they want to do is to get that pipe line into the largest market by the shortest possible route, regardless of the interests of the Canadian people. That is the position taken
Prairie Transmission Lines by these applicants for incorporation, under the name of Prairie Transmission Lines Limited; and I believe the route suggested by the Alberta Natural Gas Company would be practically the same as the one I have just described. I should be very glad if any hon. members wishing to do so would take a look at this map.
This plan means the developing of Washington and Oregon rather than British Columbia. It means also that Canada is at the end of two stub lines. There has been some talk of being able to serve Canada before the Americans are served. However, I was impressed by the evidence given by Mr. Abner Faison Dixon, who is the key man behind the other application. Giving evidence before a Senate committee last year he said, in effect, that it would be impossible for a line to run through American territory and not serve American points until Canadian points are served. If the line is to go all that way through the United States, American points will be served, make no mistake about it, and Canada is going to get what is left.
This plan means something more. The suggestion has been made that this need not be settled by parliament but left to the board of transport commissioners, about whom we have heard so much. Well, the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada have no authority whatever over that line, once it crosses the United States boundary. The only control they are going to have over this pipe line to the Pacific, if the plan of those asking for incorporation of Prairie Transmission Lines Limited is followed, will be control over two small stub lines coming up from the United States. Furthermore the consent of the federal power commission of the United States is required for the pipe line to enter that country and also for it to be laid throughout the United States. That federal power commission will be the body which will really say what is to happen and what is to be done with this pipe line.
As I pointed out before, there is no agreement between Canada and the United States that this gas will come back to British Columbia in the amounts required. I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) will not contradict that statement; he will agree that Canada has no treaty whatever with the United States concerning either oil or natural gas going from Canada across the American boundary. On that point there was some interesting evidence given last fall in the Senate committee by Mr. Dixon. He said he would think an. agreement would be insisted upon by the Canadian authorities

Prairie Transmission Lines stating that gas would unquestionably go to British Columbia in the amounts required. But there is no such agreement and last fall there had not been even any negotiations undertaken. All these difficulties would be avoided by having a Canadian main line to Vancouver. That is all the opponents of these bills are asking.
The plan set out in the map I have described has another serious feature from the point of view of western Canada. It ignores the existence of natural gas and oil in the Peace river country. This is of tremendous importance to British Columbia because these are the only oil-bearing areas in the province and they constitute the most promising part of the province from the point of view of the development of oil and natural gas resources. The route through the United States is not designed to serve the Peace river district and Mr. Dixon admitted that in his evidence last year.
The result of putting the line through the United States will be that there will be no outlet to the Pacific coast from the Peace river areas of Alberta and British Columbia and their oil and gas will be dammed back behind the oil and gas produced in the Edmonton area. That is the position those areas are in today with regard to wheat. It is a tragedy that there is no rail outlet from the Peace river to the Pacific coast. We have never been able to bring about the construction of that line and the people of the Peace river have to ship their wheat down to Edmonton rather than over a shorter route to tidewater at Prince Rupert, Vancouver or New Westminster. If this line just crosses the corner of southern British Columbia to enter the United States, Peace river oil and gas will be in the same position as their wheat. Furthermore these people have been wanting a highway. If the pipe line went through the Yellowhead pass it would tap the Peace river and provide an outlet to the south and these people would have a highway as well as a pipe line.
I was amazed to note the attitude of the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray) in this debate. For the last few weeks every time this question has come up he has been heckling and jumping up and talking about some Tory monopoly. Incidentally he never would have been elected if it had not been for Tory votes because we did not put up a candidate against him. Yet his riding stands to gain more from having a pipe line through the Yellowhead than any other riding in British Columbia.
The same is largely true of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite) who spoke a couple of weeks ago. He referred to an old
Why does not the hon. member introduce a bill?

A bill was introduced two weeks ago. I suggest to the sponsor of the Prairie Transmission Lines Limited bill, who has now come back to the chamber although he did not bother to be here late this afternoon, that he get up and pledge on behalf of the people for whom he is speaking that they will abandon their plan to put the main line through the United States and will follow an all-Canadian route; also that they will accept the amendments to their charter necessary to provide that that will be the only power given. If he does so I am confident that all opposition to his bill will cease.
If he will not do it, and if the sponsors of the Alberta Natural Gas Company will not do the same thing, then I warn members of the house that they face a fight to the finish. We have taken our stand on this question and we do not propose to step aside and see Canadians living on the Pacific slope of Canada sold down the river just to please some big interest friends of the Canadian government.

Mr. Speaker, I have not spoken on this bill before, and I am sure my friends will be glad to hear me, having just come from British Columbia
Prairie Transmission Lines today. It was raining when I left there, and we need a little oil, but strangely the people of the province of British Columbia-
Louder.
It will be louder before I have finished. I did not think the time would ever come when the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and I would be seeing eye to eye.
It is a logical tie-up.
It is a good tie-up; it is a better tie-up than you have got.

On this particular issue the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra is far more popular with the people of British Columbia than the hon. member for Coast Capilano (Mr. Sinclair). While I was home I had the privilege of being entertained at a few meetings in my riding. I did not have to call the meetings; they were called on my behalf.
They called for you.

The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing) had better go home and mend a few fences in his riding or I will quote some of the wires I have on my desk that come right from his riding. On this particular issue the people of the province of British Columbia may be a little bit selfish. I am willing to admit that, but they are not as selfish as the people of Ontario or Quebec. We may be a little selfish. We are trying to build up industry within our own province. We are trying to get some of the things to which we think we are entitled. I give every credit to the sincerity of those members from the province of British Columbia who have read speeches written in Wall street. I want them to give me credit for sincerity in what I say, and I am not reading any speech prepared for me by anybody in Wall street.
That is apparent.

I prepare my own. I can understand that my colleague would not appreciate that fact, never having made one that he wrote himself. I want to say what I think about this matter. I will be glad to let any of my colleagues take the floor for twenty minutes if they would like to, but in the meantime I am making a speech, and I am making it on behalf of the people of my riding. I have just come from there, having arrived by aeroplane today. When I got out of a taxi at the entrance to the building the division bell was ringing and there was a vote. I was pleased to be able to arrive just at the moment when a vote was being taken on that particular measure sponsored, I understand,

Prairie Transmission Lines by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), a little part of Toronto. What do they care about British Columbia?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Seconded by him.

It is the same thing. It is a little district up there. I want to assure you that they have the nicest C.P.R. station in the Dominion of Canada at Kenora in the Rainy river district, which is very well described by its name. They have a lovely station there.
It was raining in Vancouver.

I find the hon. member for Spadina, with all the great interest he has in the province of British Columbia, seconding this motion. Then I noticed the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Howe) taking a keen interest in it, and I knew perfectly well how anxious they were to hear me speak on this particular bill. I have just come back from the province of British Columbia where there are not eighteen people in the entire province who favour the United States route. There are not eighteen people in the entire province. Probably I am in a more fortunate position than other members from the province of British Columbia because I happen to represent the best riding within the province. Each and every one of the associations in my district has passed a resolution endorsing an all-Canadian route. It has been said before and was said again tonight and I will say now that, in so far as I am concerned, I will withdraw all opposition if the sponsors will come forward and say, as one company did, that they will follow an all-Canadian route.
I do not care which company builds the line but I care a great deal whether Canada is served and my province is built up.
What may surprise some hon. members who are not familiar with their own provinces is that the cheapest form of power in the world is natural gas. We have heard all about the building of new dams at Niagara for the creation of more hydroelectric power, but the cheapest form of power in the world is natural gas. The people of British Columbia want to secure some of that power. We want to do something about decentralizing industry. We are not so keen about building up Hamilton, Port Arthur and other places in Ontario as we are about building up our own province. We admire Quebec. You know, Mr. Speaker, Quebec is probably the most historic province in the dominion.
Except Newfoundland.

It is one of the most delightful to visit. The maritimes are not too bad, but probably Quebec is the most historic.


At the same time we would like to do a little building within our own province on the Pacific coast. We have every resource in. the world with the exception of oil and gas. We sincerely believe that there are oil and gas in northern British Columbia and the Peace river district. I am sorry that my good friend and colleague from that district is not here at the present moment. As has been mentioned before, I cannot understand why he prefers to see our resources developed for the benefit of the United States rather than Canada. If we develop oil and gas in our great northern country, as we think we can, we will have the richest province in the world. For that reason I can well understand there is a certain amount of jealousy in some of the provinces of central Canada. I can well understand why they would like to concentrate industry as they have in the past and prevent development on the Pacific coast, but I cannot understand some of my colleagues from our most beautiful province. I should like to say just a word or two about our province, where we have the finest climate in the world. If you were to come up to my office tonight, Mr. Speaker, I would be delighted to show you some beautiful flowers that were picked in my garden yesterday morning. When you have a province with a climate like that, a province with youthful-
Members.

Yes, they have some good members out there, too, though I am a little disappointed in one or two of them, in the amount of time they have taken while saying nothing. As I may have mentioned once or twice in this house before, I do not come from Vancouver island or Victoria; I come from the great Fraser valley, where we have everything except this natural gas. I should like to quote a little item that I saw while I was home. I am sorry I cannot say whether it is from the Sun or the Province, but they they are both good newspapers. As a matter of fact the circulation of those newspapers is among the greatest in Canada. Of course we have an advantage in that respect, because out in Coast-Capilano we have the largest pulp mill in the British empire. That riding is fairly well represented here, though not as well as during the period when I looked after it myself. This clipping contains a dispatch from Burnaby, which incidentally is one of the largest municipalities in British Columbia. At one time they had an excellent administration, particularly in their school board. It is not so good now, but they are doing their best to get by. This dispatch is headed, "Gas for B.C. before U.S., M.P.

promises." I am making no promises at all; I am just hoping for the best. The dispatch goes on:
Canadian consumers will get all the gas from Alberta they require before any is exported to the United States, Tom Goode, M.P. for Burnaby-Richmond, told fellow members of the Burnaby Lions club Thursday night.
I hope that sinks in a bit. That is not my say-so; those are the words of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode).
Talking through his hat.

The clipping goes on:
Mr. Goode said he is against a monopoly for distribution of the gas and criticized Howard Green, Vancouver-Quadra M.P. and George Cruickshank, Fraser Valley M.P., for their filibuster in the house against granting a second franchise for distribution of the gas.
The company now holding a franchise had no intention of constructing a pipe line in his opinion, said Mr. Goode.
He said Richmond municipality should not have to contribute towards the proposed Marpole bridge.
I am not interested in that just now, though I have seen many articles in the newspapers about it, and out there they say the federal government is going to spend four or five million dollars on the construction of that bridge. The hon. member promised that British Columbia would get gas before it went to the United States. Well, Mr. Speaker, the place to make such promises is right here in this chamber. There has been some talk about monopolies. We believe that in some things you must have a monopoly. I am going to make the statement definitely that, no matter what companies get franchises, only one company will build a pipe line within the next fifty years. Make no mistake about that. I do not expect to be in this chamber that long-
Why not?	.

Because I am going to move "over there". Only one company will build a pipe line, no matter how many franchises are granted. There is only one source from which the money can come. Most of it will be provided by United States investors. I understand there is another pipe line bill to be considered. I may not be in order in referring to that just now, but I will have something to say about it later on. 1 have no authority to say so, but I believe the company which some of my youthful friends permitted to get a charter last year would be agreeable to incorporating in that charter a provision that the route shall be all-Canadian. On the other hand I think it would be ridiculous to ask only one company to put that provision in its charter, without asking all the others to do the same thing. Put it in all the charters. Speaking for 55946-104
Prairie Transmission Lines myself, and I believe for certain of my friends across the way, we would be prepared to immediately withdraw our opposition if provision were made for an all-Canadian route. Why should that not be done? I should like some of my western friends in particular to study what has happened in connection with our international waterways. The records are available. I know many hon. members are busy, working hard in behalf of their constituents, but let them take time to study what happened in that connection. Once this gas or oil leaves Canada, international complications enter into it and you can have no guarantee that any portion of the gas or oil will be returned to Canada. I am surprised that some hon. members do not take advantage of the fact that we have a library in this building where they can get some information on these matters. I am surprised that some of them have never heard about the million and a half dollars expenditure under the river at Detroit, between Detroit and Windsor. By means of this, we were to get gas on the Canadian side. After that money had been expended, the United States decided there was not enough gas to supply us, so we did not get any. Let some of these people realize that there has never been one member, so far as I know, who has spoken in this so-called filibuster-we do not agree with the term- who has said that we should not export gas to the United States. Of course, we want to export our surplus gas to the United States, but we want to serve Canada first. We think it is not too much to ask some of our eastern friends to go along with us on that. Let us develop our own province and our own dominion. Let us keep a reserve within the country.
Last year, I think it was, I was heavily lobbied, as I presume the rest of the members were, in connection with processing our salmon within our own province. I have mentioned this incident before, Mr. Speaker, but it is worth repeating. These lobbyists came to me, and said we should process the fish in our own province. I think they were right. At that time the fishermen could have obtained five cents a pound more by shipping the fish to Bellingham, not far from Vancouver. These interests said, "Let us process this fish in British Columbia." Some of these same people are now saying, "Let us build a pipe line to the United States; let us build up Idaho and Washington rather than our own province of British Columbia."
These same interests, Mr. Speaker, lobbied me, and rightly so, about our timber. Incidentally, the province of British Columbia produces 55 per cent of the lumber produced

Prairie Transmission Lines in Canada. These lobbyists said that the logs should not be exported to Oregon and Washington, but should be manufactured within the province of British Columbia. I believed they were right, and I supported them. These same individuals now say that we should ship gas down to the states of Idaho and Washington. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, the greatest hydroelectric development in the entire world is at Grand Coulee, right in the area to which these people want to send natural gas. The greatest development on the Pacific coast has been ' in the states of Oregon and Washington, the spot to which they want to send this gas in order that more development may take place.
Some of us believe, Mr. Speaker, that it would be better to keep this gas within our own country, and develop our own country.
I do not like to take up the time of the house on this matter, but we feel that the sponsor of this bill should frankly state whether or not it is the intention of the company to build the line through Canada. The sponsor of one bill, on which I cannot speak, since I have already taken part in the debate on that matter, said he had not the faintest idea where the company was going to build its line. I do not think any of the members opposite hold any brief for the Westcoast Transmission Company, but that company has made a definite commitment, in the form of an application before the Alberta petroleum board, to build a Canadian route. Hon. members do not have to take my word for it; it is a matter of record. In its application, the company said it intended to build a Canadian route. Why some of these Toronto stock brokers or Wall street ambitionists could not make the same statement, I do not know. One company has made that statement in the form of a formal application before the board. So far as I am concerned, the provision covering a Canadian route could be inserted in the charters of all companies. I am speaking of the western outfit, and the people in eastern Canada can talk about Sarnia and Wisconsin.
I am primarily concerned with my own province, and western Canada. If such a provision could be inserted in the charter of every company, I would be satisfied.
It is rather difficult to talk for forty minutes when you have not a prepared script written for you by Wall street. In the first place, I am interested in talking to you people because my riding is interested. I have just returned from that riding, which is the finest riding in British Columbia. I know how the people of British Columbia feel about this matter. There are not eighteen residents in the entire province of British Columbia who favour the route to the United States. I do 

not know just what the population of the province is, but I suppose it is approximately a million. My riding has about 50,000 in it, and 48,000 of them think Cruickshank is quite smart.

about the development of Canada for Canadians rather than the development of our good friends the United States, particularly the states of Idaho and Washington. I am sure that many of my colleagues would like to say a few words in this connection in the twenty or thirty minutes at their disposal. I am sure the minister of reconstruction would like to say a few words about building Canada. There are so many new titles around here now that I am not just sure to whom I am referring when I quote the title of any particular position; but the title of minister of reconstruction intrigues me and I believe that the minister of reconstruction-
Which one?

other portion of Canada, and having had the privilege of speaking in Toronto and then in Mexico, would love to come out and tell the people of my province: "We are going to build Canada for Canadians; we are going to develop the natural resources of our own dominion for the benefit of our own people prior to assisting any other country, no matter how friendly they may be." FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
1.	What steps, if any, have been taken for the promotion of agriculture in Newfoundland, during the past year?
2.	What work, if any, is to be done during the coming fiscal year for the same purpose?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
1.	The Department of Agriculture has been working in co-operation with the department of natural resources of Newfoundland in taking over those activities which normally are performed by the federal department. Responsibility for inspection of animals for contagious diseases was taken over during the past year. An inspector was also appointed to examine for disease and insect pests plants and plant products entering Newfoundland. The provincial entomologist was also transferred to the federal staff.
Officers of the federal department were sent to conduct surveys during the summer of 1949 for plant diseases and insect pests. A soil specialist was also sent over to consult with the Newfoundland soil survey staff. Several other officials went to Newfoundland in connection with discussions on grading and inspection of agricultural products.
The sum of $251,168.94 was paid in freight assistance on the moving of 12,554 tons of feed grain to Newfoundland. It is expected that about $2,000 will be paid toward meeting the cost of agricultural limestone.
2.	Effective April 1, 1950, the demonstration farm, formerly operated by the Newfoundland government, became part of the experimental farm service of the federal Department of Agriculture. This involved the transfer of buildings, livestock and equipment and a staff of five employees. This farm will now be operated to give the same type of service as federal experimental farms in other provinces. This will include research and demonstration on improved agricultural methods.
Discussions have been taking place with the Newfoundland authorities concerning the inspection of fruits and vegetables, poultry and eggs, and dairy products. It is expected that the Newfoundland authorities will co-operate in establishment of this type of work during the present fiscal year.
Newfoundland has asked the agricultural economics division of marketing service to conduct a survey during the coming summer on the marketing of farm products in Newfoundland. The survey will be under the direction of officers of the federal department, and the staff will be drawn from both federal and provincial employees.
