subtopic: SUGGESTED APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CHOOSE A DISTINCTIVE FLAG

speakeroldname: Mr. J. T. Richard (Ottawa East) moved:
subtopic: SUGGESTED APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CHOOSE A DISTINCTIVE FLAG
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, consideration should be given to the appointment of a special committee to report upon the choice of a distinctive Canadian flag.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving this resolution I should like to point out that the flag question has been discussed on many occasions in former parliaments. In 1924 the government appointed a committee of officials to select a design for a Canadian flag. There were debates on the subject in 1931, 1932, 1933, 1935, 1937 and 1938. In that year the prime minister, Right Hon. Mr. King, and the then leader of the opposition, Right Hon. Mr. Bennett, agreed that a committee should be appointed to recommend an appropriate design. Then there was an important debate on a resolution introduced in 1939 by Mr. Cameron McIntosh, and in 1942 a private bill was introduced by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix). However, the most important discussion on the subject in recent years took place in 1945, when the then prime minister moved for the appointment of a committee to consider and report upon a suitable design for a Canadian flag, which committee sat in 1945 and 1946.
Perhaps it is well to point out that Canada does not possess a national flag other than the union jack, except to the extent that orders in council of 1924 and 1945 permitted the use of the red ensign under certain circumstances.
The first question which arises is as follows: For what does a distinctive flag for Canada stand? Mr. Speaker, borrowing some of the words used by Mr. McIntosh, I would give the following definition. I believe a distinctive flag for Canada would stand for

individual freedom; national freedom; national unity; the rallying force in the defence of the nation in times of emergency; the common sentiment of the Canadian people; our past history; our past resolutions; our past achievements; the ideals which will lead us to overcome all that is ignoble, untrue, and all that is of a defeatist nature in the days to come. It would also exemplify the coronation oath which was taken in 1937 by His Majesty, as King of Canada. It would stand for the equality of Canada with the United Kingdom, and the building up of the commonwealth of nations. It would stand for the Statute of Westminster of 1931, by which Canada was designated not as a colony but as a sovereign nation within the ambit of the British commonwealth. It would stand also for our devotion to Canada; our national defence; our national pride, honour and glory.
Since we have acquired the right to amend our own constitution, to decide the appeals from our courts in Canada, it should stand also for our new independence. It should stand for our newly acquired prestige since the second great war, both within the commonwealth and amongst the great nations of the world. Mr. Speaker, may I remind this house that at the January conference, all the premiers of the provinces of Canada, as well as the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), reasserted the fact of Canada's independence in the commonwealth, and the desirability of making any provincial or federal amendments to the constitution entirely within Canada and by Canadian means.
A distinctive flag asserts nationality, whether it is flown afloat or ashore. When flown officially in foreign countries, it indicates the occupancy of embassies and consulates by the country of the flag. When flown at international gatherings, it shows that its country is present; and when flown at international sport meets, it is shown to indicate the winner of athletic events. Without a national flag a country cannot be recognized as being present.
A distinctive national flag engenders patriotism in the hearts of the people, and it raises enthusiasm for its country in the minds of those who see it. It teaches all, and especially the young, to love their own country or to support their country; it constitutes a rallying point in times of stress, and brings strength and respect. A distinctive Canadian flag should engender and bolster unity among the people of Canada. At no time in our history has this sentiment of unity been greater than it is now. The people of this country are seeking for a
Canadian Flag
symbol to which they can look with devotion and pride, and which will represent the ideals and the qualities of a citizen of this great country.
The next question which might be raised is whether the time is appropriate. Even in 1945 the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, in moving the resolution, made this statement:
There have been suggestions by some persons that this is not an important matter, and that it should not be brought forward at this time. With this I emphatically disagree. In the life of every nation symbols are important, and perhaps the most important of them is a national flag. We need only to think of the vast affection and loyalty that has attached to the Union Jack in Britain and throughout the commonwealth, and I yield to no one in the house in my admiration for that great symbol of empire. In the same way, for our neighbours to the south the stars and stripes have been an inspiration to national unity and national endeavour. We in Canada have shared the Union Jack, and we shall always honour it as the symbol of much that is best and most precious ini our heritage; but we have had nothing that has b'een peculiarly and indisputably our own, that would symbolize Canada -all of Canada and everyone in Canada. There should be something that all can see and look to with pride, as the symbol of this great nation of ours, to which affection and loyalty can attach, and which can become the sign of the unity and purpose that will make Canada great.
I agree particularly with the last statement of the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, Mr. Speaker, and especially that one which relates to affection and loyalty to Canada, for at no time has it been more evident than now that it is necessary to instil into the minds and hearts of our people a strong feeling of loyalty, faith and devotion in Canada and its democratic institutions. Canadians must be united, not only in defence but in the development of the vast natural and spiritual resources which we possess. All other nations in the commonwealth have their own national flags, some of which are distinctive, and the lack of such a flag by Canadians created some unhappy incidents during the war; at international meetings; at Olympic and other sport events; at public demonstrations in Canada and elsewhere. We can be loyal to the King of Canada, and still own a distinctive Canadian flag. I do not think that there are any subjects more truly loyal to His Majesty in any part of the commonwealth at present than in Canada, and this is evidenced by the great attachment and devotion, not only to Their Majesties themselves but also to their popular representatives, Viscount and Lady Alexander.
The Hon. Paul Martin at the first meeting of the Canadian flag committee in 1945 said:
There has been too little, not too much, national pride in that country. We are part of a great commonwealth organization that has been an example to the world, and we have every intention of

Canadian Flag
remaining a part, and of helping it on to greater and better things. We hope for much from the new United Nations Organization, in which we feel that we will play our full and active part. Our gaze is turning more and more outward, and in carrying our responsibilities in the new world, we will be better fitted to do our part if we have an essential feeling of internal unity and oneness. That is why, I think, it is important to give greater emphasis to the Canadian aspect of things, and1 why it is desirable that the work of this committee should result in an acceptable and appropriate design.
Mr. Speaker, we do not think of one who has a well-developed sense of local pride in his own city as lacking in his own patriotism, nor should we think of one who has a good sense of Canadian pride as being only the least devoted to the purposes and principles of the commonwealth of nations. Mr: Speaker, I believe it will be the responsibility of the present parliament to select a distinctive Canadian flag. I believe that all the parties represented in this house, at their national conventions in recent years, have passed resolutions in favour of the selection of a flag which will mark the spirit, pride, loyalty and devotion of Canadians to our country.
It would, of course, be much better to delay the adoption of a flag than to decide now upon the selection of one that is not so distinctive. In moving this resolution, I wanted it to be clearly understood that in accepting it this house would be accepting the broad definition that I have outlined as to what is a distinctive Canadian flag, namely, that it should not contain the emblems, symbols or designs of any other national flag, whether in whole or in part. I would, of course, much prefer to have this resolution in the hands of the government where it belongs, but I hope that this house will agree with me that I am expressing the wish of the majority of the Canadian people in asking for an opinion of the members regarding the formation of a committee to select a distinctive Canadian flag.
Mr. Speaker, I hope there will soon be a distinctive Canadian flag, a new symbol born to mark all that is good and all that is great in Canada; one that we can transmit to our children so that they may wave it cheerfully, salute with pride and defend, if need be with their lives, for the great privilege it represents of being Canadians.
As Mr. Ilsley said in closing his remarks in 1945:
I earnestly hope that It will be unanimously adopted by the house, and that the work of the committee will settle now and for all, and for the good of Canada, and through the growth and influence of Canada, for the good of the commonwealth and the community of nations, this question of our national flag and symbol. The children of today and, let us pray, the children of tomorrow,

will strive for and gain a new peace, a new freedom and a new security under the protection of the flag of Canada.

subtopic: SUGGESTED APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CHOOSE A DISTINCTIVE FLAG
speechtext:
I wish to say a few words, Mr. Speaker, in support of the resolution of my colleague the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard). For many years there has been a growing sentiment in every part of Canada in favour of a distinctive national flag for Canada. Although a young nation, Canada finds herself today one of the most important powers of the world. In the course of the last half century our country has had to its credit great achievements from which Canadians derive a growing national pride and this pride translates itself, as we can feel more and more as time passes, into a distinctive Canadian spirit in every section of our country.
May I remind you, sir, that at one time some of us French-speaking Canadians were under the impression that this distinctive Canadian spirit was limited to the population living within the boundaries of the province of Quebec. But if that ever was the case, such a situation does not exist any longer. At this point I wish to warn my French-speaking compatriots from the province of Quebec against an error which is far too common among certain classes of our French-speaking population who are too often inclined to take it for granted that the only real and true Canadians in this country are those of French descent, the other part of the Canadian population being labelled or earmarked as "les Anglais", the English.
I have sat in this house long enough now to know beyond any doubt that the great majority of our English-speaking colleagues, whatever their political affiliations, are just as true, sincere and good Canadians as any of our French-speaking colleagues in this house; and the people who have elected them to this parliament must also share most of their views on most of our national issues. May I also add that the election of a Frenchspeaking Canadian Prime Minister, with such an overwhelming majority, at the last general election, makes it obvious that this truly distinctive Canadian spirit exists outside the province of Quebec as well as within the boundaries of that province. As a result, never before in our history has there been a time when the great majority of Canadians, English-speaking as well as French-speaking, were ever prouder of being Canadians. Except perhaps for certain countries controlled by the communists, wherever in the world a Canadian may go today he is welcomed, greeted and respected as a Canadian as soon as he identifies himself as such. The time has therefore come when Canadians, proud as they are of Canada, their homeland, should

be given a distinctive sign by which they can easily, promptly and fully identify themselves at first sight as Canadians. The time is now ripe, Mr. Speaker, when this country should be given a distinctive national flag by which she can identify herself and distinguish herself from other parts of the world as well as from other nations of the commonwealth, a Canadian flag distinguished from any other national flag in the world; a Canadian flag that would make every Canadian boy and girl live not for the country from which his or her ancestors came one, two, three, nine or ten generations ago but live Cor, work for, fight for and be ready to die for Canada, his or her sacred native land.
My colleague the hon. member for Ottawa East has quoted a statement made by the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley. May I quote what the leader of the C.C.F. party, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), stated in this house on November 8, 1945, as reported at page 1939 of Hansard:
1 wish to see Canada with a distinctive flag, and in my opinion the red ensign with a coat of arms on it, which I would rather say nothing about, is not a distinctive flag . . . The flag of the British commonwealth is the union jack, and we respect it, but I am pleased indeed to know that my hon. friends to the right are prepared to recognize that the time has come when Canada should have a flag of her own.
Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, the then prime minister of Canada, stated in this house on February 14, 1938, as reported at page 438 of Hansard:
The use of the union jack on anything that is distinctively Canadian in the United States does not help to emphasize the individuality of this country or its distinct nationality; it helps to submerge them altogether.
And finally, our present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), then minister of justice, stated in this house on November 13, 1945, as reported at page 2097 of Hansard:
The purpose for which it is suggested there should be a distinctive national flag is ... to have a symbol that all Canadians can look upon as distinctively their own, not because they want to discard the union jack, but because the union jack is not distinctively their own and because they feel that their nation has now reached the stature in the family of nations that requires it to have something which can be regarded as its own.
I am sorry that we have no such statement from the leader of the Progressive Conservative party or any of his lieutenants. It has been suggested before in this house that the Canadian population was not quite prepared to accept at the present time a distinctive national flag as well as a national anthem of our own.
It has been said also that more time was needed before a government could face those
Medals and Decorations two issues without arousing controversy which might endanger national unity in this country. Who will ever know the answers to those questions until such time as the Canadian people have had an opportunity to express themselves with respect to them?
Therefore I say that unless proper legislation is introduced and adopted by the house to give our country a national and distinctive flag, and an official national anthem, and within a reasonable time, a referendum should be held on those two questions. This should be done at the earliest possible convenient moment.
This procedure has been taken before. In 1941 a referendum was held on a controversial issue. This is the only accurate and democratic way of learning the will of the majority of the Canadian people with respect to those important subjects. I for one hold the sincere conviction that if such a referendum were held today in Canada concerning those two issues, in all provinces of Canada, without exception, the yeas would have it.
Motion agreed to.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR FORMULATION OF NATIONAL PROGRAM
REQUEST FOR FORMULATION OF NATIONAL PROGRAM
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of seeking the cooperation, of the provinces for the purpose of formulating a program of social security that will be national in scope, adequate in its provisions, and that will cover all the people of Canada in every circumstance where the individual or the family is, for reasons beyond their control, deprived of earning a living.
He said: Mr. Speaker, if I thought this resolution would have as easy a time as the two immediately preceding it, my comments in proposing it would be brief indeed. However, I am afraid the government is not so ready to accept an over-all social security program, such as I am now suggesting, as it is, if one may judge by the two preceding motions, to accept a distinctive Canadian flag and to set up a committee to look into the granting of medals. If it were as ready in the present instance to accept my suggestion, there would be no real necessity for a long debate.
At the last session of parliament I introduced a resolution substantially similar to this one. I believe it was moved on October 3, 1949. On that occasion I made what I thought was a reasoned case for the enactment of an over-all social security program for Canada.
Tonight, first of all, I should like to reply to some of the criticisms of my resolution of last year made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). May I first of all draw attention to the fact that the resolution I introduced last session was found to be out of order because of the wording, and with that in mind I have this year made the slight amendment necessary to bring my resolution strictly within the rules of the house.
My resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of seeking the cooperation of the provinces for the purpose of formulating a program of social security that will be national in scope, adequate in its provisions, and that will cover all the people of Canada in every circumstance where the individual or the family is, for reasons beyond their control, deprived of earning a living.
Because of the criticism offered by the Minister of National Health and Welfare I have in my present resolution made a slight change in the third to last line. One of the reasons given by the minister for refusing to accept my resolution was that in it I had asked that social security apply to every citizen of Canada. He pointed out that there were many

Canadians who do not live in Canada, and that for that reason he could not accept my resolution. I think that criticism was on a par with his other criticisms. They were petty, niggling objections. If I had attempted to cover all the people in Canada I have no doubt that he would say he could not accept it because of that. I do not suppose that I could formulate a resolution that would be so word perfect that the minister could not find fault with it. I imagine he would find fault with any resolution unless the government was ready to accept it.
However, it will be noted that the resolution in its purpose is the same as the one introduced last year. It asks the government to seek the co-operation of the provinces. I should like to quote from page 481 of Hansard of October 3, 1949, where the minister is reported as follows:
Then, another objection I see to these very doubtful terms is that the resolution as a whole takes no account whatsoever of municipal responsibility.
Surely when the minister made that statement he must have realized that I have been long enough in this house to know that if I were to ask the government to seek the co-operation of the municipalities I would be told by the Minister of National Health and Welfare that they are the creation of the provinces and for that reason this government could have no dealings with them. I point that out to the minister because I know that would be his stock answer if at any time I had made the suggestion which he found fault with me for not making. The minister went on to say:
Then again-and I have to interpret the resolution very strictly, because of its implications-this resolution in its final terms does not take into consideration a citizen or individual who might himself be guilty of an act which would put him out of the wage-earning market, or the income-earning market -and there are a few such individuals. A man could deliberately-and we have had such cases- dismember his two hands, and yet under this resolution he would be entitled to benefits.
I submit that that is a new low in criticism, even for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. As a matter of fact under the law in Canada today a person would receive compensation, even if his injury were caused by his own negligence or even worse. Even if that were not the law, does any member of this house suppose that if Tom Jones or Bill Doe or somebody else were to cut off his two hands-that is a far-fetched mutilation- he would be allowed to starve? Decidedly not. If a man takes another's life we feed and look after him until we put him out of the way by legal processes, and we would clothe and shelter this other man and provide someone to feed him because he would not be able to feed himself. As I say, this

is a new low in criticism of a resolution put forward in a serious manner. The minister went on to say:
The final observation I would make in this particular is to indicate, as I said at the outset, that there is no country in the world with a provision of this kind. Take a country where, it may be suggested, social security benefits are most comprehensive-and it has been suggested the United Kingdom is such a country; for the purposes of argument let us accept that suggestion. But in the United Kingdom there is no social security measure which provides social security assistance for all citizens of the United Kingdom in every circumstance where an individual or family is for any reason deprived of the opportunity of earning a living.
I submit that there is such legislation in the old country and I submit that there is even such legislation in Canada. It may not be adequate, but any person not able to provide for himself is now provided for either by federal, provincial or municipal legislation. But any reasonable deduction from the terms of the motion and the words used to explain it would be that what I was proposing was that we should integrate our program so that every individual, be he citizen or resident- I will go that far with the minister-shall be entitled to food, clothing and shelter if he is unable to provide himself with these things for reasons beyond his own control.
That is the essence of our social legislation, to make provision for those people who for reasons beyond their control are no longer able to provide for themselves. Sooner or later we will reach the position where that provision will be made on a more adequate and orderly scale than at present. I am sure that if the minister did not find himself in the position where he had to reply to a resolution which he knew the government would not accept he would agree with that point of view. I think I can leave the minister's criticism there. I was sorry I did not get an opportunity to reply to him at the time, but perhaps his criticism is not worthy of a reply even now.
There are one or two other points I wish to make. When I introduced the resolution last session-and I appreciate that the minister noticed my effort to avoid as far as possible, and it was completely possible, the making of political insinuations or the drawing of political comparisons-I had one purpose in view, and that was to get the principles of the resolution accepted by the house. I also pointed out that I knew all the tricks if I merely wanted to make political capital.
When the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), who followed me in the debate, began his remarks he made a statement to the effect-I have not got his speech before me-that C.C.F. members alwav-
Social Security
made it appear that they were the only people who were interested in social security matters. I do not believe that any C.C.F. member takes that position. Certainly I did not take that position in introducing the resolution, but even if I or other members of the C.C.F. had done so members of the Progressive Conservative party should be the last to accuse us. My memory of the Conservative party, and it goes back for more years than I care to admit, is that they have considered themselves as being the real guardians of all the true patriotism in this country. But as a matter of fact, not only does the C.C.F. take the lead in these matters, but it is admitted by people who are opponents of the C.C.F. that we do lead.
I am going to put two or three references on record tonight for those who might care to try to refute them. We have had considerable discussion about old age pensions during the present session, and I imagine we will have more before the session is over. During my part in that debate I made reference to the many times that I have heard old age pensions discussed in the house. In 1931, under the government of the late R. B. Bennett, we had a fairly long debate on how the old age pension legislation came to be enacted. I wish to read to the house a short statement made by the then prime minister, Mr. Bennett, which will be found at page 4200 of Hansard for that year. Referring to a speech that had been made by the then leader of the opposition, the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, he said:
What would the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) have said if when the bill was introduced he had listened to the speech he has listened to this afternoon? What would he have thought? He was the man who forced this upon a reluctant administration.
He was referring to the old age pension.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre never made any bones about what he wanted, he was frank and open about it, and he said, "the necessity of one party is my opportunity, and I am going to press it to the full for the benefit of my friends." And he did.
When you find a man with as little sympathy for the C.C.F. as the late Viscount Bennett making a statement of that kind you can accept it that the statement is correct. I should like to quote now from an editorial that appeared in a publication which has never shown any partiality towards the C.C.F. The editorial I now have in my hand appeared in Maclean's magazine of August 1, 1948, following three federal by-elections which were won by the C.C.F. in May and June of that year. The editorial reads:
Old line politicians are talking too much, and doing too little, about the recent victories of the C.C.F. To listen to some of them, you'd think the

The resolution which is now before the house, in the amended form in which it has been presented, certainly has a more desirable content than it had before. In spite of the criticisms which have been levelled by the hon. member who has just spoken regarding my objection to it in the form in which it was discussed in this house a few months ago, I cannot deny that one of the underlying benefits of the resolution is that it calls upon the government to consider the advisability of seeking the co-operation of the provinces for the purpose of formulating a program of social security that will be national in scope and adequate in its provisions.
A great deal of the discussion that has taken place in this house with regard to the matter of social security envisages a responsibility to be borne entirely by the central government. Speaking on behalf of the government on a number of occasions, I have sought to indicate that our belief with regard to the implementation of a social security program is predicated upon the conviction that, in a federal state like Canada, we must have the co-operation of the provinces, not only in the formulating of programs but in the administration of them. I hope that the resolution which has been introduced by the hon. gentleman will serve to dissipate the opinion that exists in many quarters that the party to which my hon. friend belongs believes that social services should be maintained entirely by the federal

government. His resolution does not envisage that; and, because it does not, I am glad to be able to give with regard to that particular portion of the resolution a word of commendation.

I can only take that as another indication that he is not himself satisfied about the validity of family allowances as a social security measure. On Wednesday the government, through the Department of National Health and Welfare, will be discussing with the ten provinces, through the dominion council of health, important matters affecting the health of the people of this country. Every year-twice a year, as a matter of fact-we sit down in Ottawa with the provincial departments of health, discussing ways and means of making more effective the kind of co-operation which my hon. friend says that we should seek in attempts to formulate more adequate programs of social security. Two weeks ago we sat down 
again with representatives of all the provinces to further the development of our physical fitness program. On May 25 we are sitting down with all the provinces to discuss the whole problem of rehabilitation of the handicapped of this country, at a conference that has been summoned as a result of the invitation extended by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare. All along, in almost everything we are doing in this field, we are seeking continually the co-operation of the provinces because we believe that while there are some matters such as workmen's compensation and mothers' allowances that traditionally have been initiated, and are now being administered, by the provinces, there are other matters that can more effectively be undertaken as a result of joint co-operation.
Old age pensions is one of those. That represents a joint co-operative effort. That act came into being on an enabling basis and its effective provisions were made possible only in the light of action that was taken subsequently, as a result of basic legislation passed by this parliament, followed by provincial action; and that act has not been without significance. Unemployment insurance came into being as a result of the determination of this government to do what this resolution suggests, to seek the co-operation of the provinces. Under the Unemployment Insurance Act we had no power under the constitution to deal with the matter of compulsory contributions to make unemployment insurance effective. To bring that about, we asked the provinces if they would endow the federal government with the necessary constitutional power to enact the Unemployment Insurance Act. That consent was given and we now have the Unemployment Insurance Act. But the important consideration for the point that I am making now is to realize that that legislation came about as a result of co-operation between the dominion government on the one hand and the provincial governments on the other; and in the process of that collaboration we have developed, in spite of what the hon. gentleman persists in saying to the contrary, a social security program in this country of which we have every reason to be proud. That does not mean to say that it is perfect; but to underestimate it is not to act in a responsible way. Our total national expenditures now amount to $2,400 million. Of that sum we are spending for

health and social welfare on federal and provincial accounts over $850 million. I ask my hon. friend who has just spoken-
